paras: The lynching of John Hartfield took place on June 26, 1919, near Ellisville, Mississippi, where a crowd hanged Hartfield, a Black man accused of assaulting a young white woman, and burned his body. He had been badly wounded at his capture, and the Black press covered the case widely, largely because Governor Theodore G. Bilbo had said beforehand that he was "utterly powerless" to stop it.

Hartfield was accused of assaulting a young white woman of Ellisville, in Jones County; wire reports called him her "confessed assailant." Posses trailed him for about ten days through three counties, and according to the wire reports they included several hundred Black men. A Laurel dispatch said that during the hunt a white man was killed, three Black men who "had absolutely nothing to do with the crime" were shot, and many Black men and women were beaten.

According to the New York Age, bloodhounds tracked Hartfield to a schoolhouse at Hot Coffee, near Collins, where he fired at the posse and two farmers, Walter Crawley and Will Rogers, shot him with buckshot. Other reports said he was found in a canebrake; he was captured at daybreak on June 26 and taken by automobile to Ellisville. Guarded by a committee of citizens, he was examined by Dr. A. J. Carter, who said he could not live twenty-four hours, and the woman identified him there.

Meanwhile committee members piled crossties and brush near the railroad trestle, and word spread of a hanging at the big gum tree. Taken from the doctor's office despite the guards' pleas to wait, Hartfield was hanged from the gum tree where he was said to have held the woman. Men in the crowd fired pistols at the body during its death struggles, and burning fagots reduced it to ashes within an hour. The Laurel dispatch put the crowd at more than 5,000 and said members cut off his fingers and toes as souvenirs.

The woman and her mother watched, and people in the crowd subscribed more than $1,000 for her. No arrests were made, and the authorities called the lynching "orderly." Bilbo had answered petitions to prevent it by saying the state had no troops and "nobody can keep the inevitable from happening," and the Attorney General held the matter outside federal jurisdiction.

The NAACP's annual conference petitioned Vice President Thomas R. Marshall for federal troops in Mississippi, citing Bilbo's statement. Harry E. Davis of the association's Cleveland branch received by mail a photograph of Hartfield hanging, with the note, "This is the way we'll give you your rights." Bilbo later told the New York World it was "practically impossible" to prevent the lynching of "Negro rapists" and blamed the Northern Black press.

Coverage began on June 28 with wire briefs in the National Advocate and the Colorado Statesman that repeated the phrase "confessed assailant." Some July 5 papers kept the wire's language: the Richmond Planet headlined "Confessed Assailant of Mississippi Girl Is Put to Death By Mob," and the Ohio State Monitor ran the Laurel dispatch twice. By contrast, the New York Age headlined "Dying Man Is Hanged and Burned by Fiends in Mississippi" and called the posse "bloodthirsty violators of the law." The Chicago Defender's "White Heathens Burn Man's Body to Ashes" quoted a woman in the crowd who called a false assault charge "a good way to get money."

Editorials focused on the governor: the St. Louis Argus urged Bilbo's impeachment, and the New York Age called for a federal anti-lynching law with "teeth in it." The Richmond Planet argued the law would have executed Hartfield and later ranked his death among the six worst lynchings of 1919, while the Omaha Monitor and the Dallas Express also condemned Bilbo.

Most accounts placed the hanging at a gum tree, but the first wire brief and a New York Age editorial said the railroad trestle, and two papers named Laurel. The Cleveland Gazette's correspondent wrote that the fire was set "while he hung and kicked," whereas the Laurel dispatch said he was believed dead when hanged.

reader.title: Lynching of John Hartfield
bases: Hartfield, accused of assaulting a white woman, was taken from guards by a crowd, hanged, shot and burned near Ellisville (A16, A17, A14).

A crowd put at more than 5,000 took Hartfield from the doctor's office without legal process and hanged, shot and burned him (A14, A17), as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A1, A16).
Separate wire dispatches from Ellisville and Laurel and a Black correspondent agree that Hartfield was captured wounded, hanged and burned (A16, A14, A7).

accounts.label: Wire report (Ellisville)
accounts.gist: Hartfield, the 'confessed assailant', was captured wounded after a ten-day hunt, identified by the woman at a doctor's office, and hanged at a gum tree and burned in an 'orderly' lynching; posses included Black men.

accounts.label: Laurel dispatch
accounts.gist: After a manhunt in which a white man was killed and three uninvolved Black men were shot, Hartfield was taken from guards, beaten, hanged (believed already dead), shot and burned before more than 5,000 people, who took fingers and toes as souvenirs.

accounts.label: New York Age capture account
accounts.gist: Gantt bloodhounds tracked him to a schoolhouse at Hot Coffee near Collins, where he fired at the posse and was shot through a window by two farmers.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Youngstown)
accounts.gist: Caught in a canebrake and shot, he was hanged above a woodpile and the fire was set while he was still alive.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: He was burned at the stake under a chaplain's supervision, after which $1,000 was given to the woman who made the charge.

accounts.label: Governor Bilbo
accounts.gist: Before the lynching he said the state had no troops and could not stop it; afterward he said lynching 'Negro rapists' was practically impossible to prevent and blamed Northern Black papers and associations.

framing.detail: National Advocate, Colorado Statesman and Richmond Planet ran wire copy calling him the 'confessed assailant' and the woman 'his victim' ('Confessed Assailant of Mississippi Girl Is Put to Death By Mob').
New York Age: 'Dying Man Is Hanged and Burned by Fiends in Mississippi', 'bloodthirsty violators of the law', the 'alleged victim' an enthusiastic witness.
Chicago Defender: 'White Heathens Burn Man's Body to Ashes', with a crowd member's remark implying false assault charges.
Editorials in the St. Louis Argus, New York Age and Richmond Planet attacked Bilbo, urged impeachment and federal anti-lynching law.
Ohio State Monitor printed (twice) a Laurel dispatch under 'Hatfiled Lynched in Laurel Miss.', including the souvenir-taking.

sources.note: Earliest wire brief, Ellisville June 27: 'confessed assailant' wounded by farmers, hanged to a girder of the railroad trestle.
quotes: John Hartfield, negro, confessed assailant of a young white woman, was lynched here by a mob.

sources.note: Wire brief: trailed ten days by posses including several hundred Black men; captured in a canebrake, hanged to a gum tree and burned; woman witnessed.
Editorial: urges impeachment of Bilbo, removal of the sheriff 'who allowed the prisoner to be taken', federal interference.
quotes: The good people of Mississippi should impeach Governor Bilbo for violation of his oath of office.

sources.note: New York state guard recruiting item citing Bilbo's 'utterly impossible' remark.
'White Heathens Burn Man's Body to Ashes': burned at the stake under a chaplain's supervision; $1,000 raised; crowd woman's remark; hundreds preparing to leave.
quotes: I have discovered a good way to get money. Just make an outfit that you have been assaulted by a Negro.

sources.note: NAACP conference report: petition to Vice President Marshall for federal troops in Mississippi, citing Bilbo on the Hartfield lynching 'Thursday'.
Youngstown correspondent's brief: caught in a canebrake, fire set 'while he hung and kicked'; text cut off.
quotes: Then they hung him to a tree above a pile of wood and set fire to the wood while he hung and kicked.

sources.note: ANP comment on Bilbo's 'inevitable' remark about the lynching of 'a dying man'; OCR heavily garbled.
Front-page headline block: 'Dying Man Is Hanged and Burned by Fiends in Mississippi'.
Opening of Age story ('Italisville'): trailed by Gantt bloodhounds, captured wounded at daybreak June 26, hanged to a gum tree, body burned.
Continuation (mixed with an insurance story): alleged victim an 'enthusiastic' witness; 'ORDERLY'; committee guard; Dr. A. J. Carter's 24-hour prognosis.
quotes: The lynching and burning was conducted in a manner which the authorities characterized as "ORDERLY."

sources.note: Continuation: crossties piled near trestle; capture at a Hot Coffee schoolhouse; farmers Walter Crawley and Will Rogers shot him with buckshot.
Editorial 'The Failure of Law': Bilbo's plea, Attorney General's no-jurisdiction view; calls for a federal anti-lynching law.
Laurel dispatch June 27: manhunt casualties, lynching at 3 p.m., 5,000 witnesses, body shot and burned, fingers and toes taken as souvenirs.
quotes: The negro's fingers and toes were cut off by members of the crowd for souvenirs.
More than 5000 persons witnessed the lynching of Hartfield.

sources.note: Editorial 'That Horrible Lynching': near Collins June 26; colored men aided; law would have executed him.
Fullest wire dispatch, Ellisville June 26: ten-day hunt, capture near Collins, committee guard, doctor's office, identification.
quotes: posse leaders freely admitted they rendered valuable assistance during the chase, knowing when they enlisted that it was intended to lynch the fugitive when he was caught.

sources.note: Continuation 'Hanged to Big Gum Tree': noose, hanging, pistol shots at the body, burning to ashes.
quotes: While the body was in its death struggles, pistols were produced by the men in the crowd and fired point-blank at the swinging form.

sources.note: Continuation: woman and mother witnessed; $1,000 subscribed; no arrests; Bilbo 'utterly powerless'.
quotes: No arrests were made after the Lynching and tonight the little town was quiet.
